name: Moldova
summary_text: Moldova's statutory framework is comparatively strong for the region. Anti-LGBT hate speech and hate crimes have been criminal offences since 2022 with sexual orientation and gender identity named explicitly, and the equality law was amended in 2023 to cover both grounds. A 2024 legislative analysis by ECOM, benchmarked against international standards and built on a survey of local partner organisations, still identifies gaps affecting LGBT people and people living with HIV in access to justice and in the operation of hate-crime and discrimination provisions.  Enforcement lags the statute. The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 records hate speech as a serious problem with no meaningful state response, a finding echoed in the European Commission's country report, and notes that political hate speech rose during the election period. Amnesty International's 2025 reporting states that discrimination against LGBTI people remained commonplace and that freedom of expression and assembly was arbitrarily restricted, with impunity persisting for past violations.  Document-related discrimination has been adjudicated. In 2023 the Equality Council confirmed that a trans woman had been denied bank service because her documents did not match her appearance, and recommended preventive measures; the case indicates that a mismatch between identity papers and presentation can be raised successfully before a national body, but that the underlying practice persists.  Hostility is measurable in social-distance data cited by GENDERDOC-M from the Equality Council's study "Prejudices and Marginalization in Moldova 2022", published in January 2023: 79% of respondents would not accept LGBT+ neighbours, 60% would not accept them as work colleagues, and marginalisation of LGBT+ people increased during 2022.  Public assembly proceeds, with a documented record of state protection and of state failure. Moldova Pride 2024 in Chisinau was attended by participants of all ages and backgrounds and proceeded openly. In 2018 police deployed tear gas against anti-LGBT protesters attempting to disrupt the march in Chisinau, and activists at the time feared a repeat of earlier violent scenes. In 2013 the Balti Court of Appeals ruled on 28 February that the "gay propaganda" ban adopted by the northern city was unconstitutional and violated human rights, striking down church-led local bans introduced after protests against the EU-backed anti-discrimination law.  Detention is the sharpest documented risk. Igor Brumarețchi, a transgender man registered female at birth in 1972 whose documents were changed to male in 2007, served a four-year sentence in Moldova's penitentiary system, mostly at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca, held alone in unsanitary, rat-infested cells for long periods in the disciplinary isolation unit, supposedly for his own safety. His request to be placed in sector 12, the unit for detainees requiring protection, was refused. He describes forced strip searches, gynaecology calls over the intercom, staff opening his bathroom door, and being addressed by a female name at roll-call, and states that only self-harm and hunger strikes caused him to be heard. The case amounts to de facto placement of a trans detainee by birth sex in the men's system, prolonged solitary-style isolation, refused protection-ward placement, and no special-unit option. The National Penitentiary Administration replied that he was held alone at his own written request, that no rights were violated, and that the discrimination claims were unconfirmed. Ziarul de Gardă notified the Ombudsman and GENDERDOC-M of the case; Brumarețchi says he will sue in Moldovan courts and the ECtHR.  Reporting from Soroca district in April 2025 corroborates the same case: Brumarețchi, from Dubna village, spent three years locked alone in a cell at Penitentiary No. 6, fully isolated from other detainees and humiliated by staff on grounds of sexual orientation, which brought him to the edge of suicide. The authorities acknowledged that homophobia persists in state institutions and said they are training staff and preparing stricter penalties for discrimination and harassment.  One part of the country operates under a materially worse regime: in Russian-occupied Transnistria, new legislation prohibits promotion of "non-traditional sexual relations".
